utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today, on Monday, the 10th of November, 2008, I would first of all like to greet the accused, the Defence teams, Mr. Scott and his associates, as well as everyone else assisting us. There is an oral decision I would like to read out. It is a bit long, and I will read it out slowly. Oral decision on the request to reconsider the oral decision rendered by the Chamber on the 16th of October, 2008, regarding a new subject addressed in the course of the Petkovic Defence cross-examination. The witness, Mirko Zelenika, testified from the 14th to the 16th of October, 2008. On the 15th of October, 2008, the Petkovic Defence, through Ms. Alaburic, cross-examined the witness Zelenika. On the 16th of October, 2008, in its oral decision, the Trial Chamber decided that the time used for the cross-examination conducted by Ms. Alaburic to deal with a new subject would be deducted from the overall amount of time allocated to the Petkovic Defence. On the very same day, Ms. Alaburic asked the Chamber to be more precise with regard to the oral decision and contested it. On the 20th of October, 2008, at the hearing, the Prosecution responded to the Petkovic Defence request, and on that same day the Petkovic Defence responded to the Prosecution. On the 30th of October, 2008, the Petkovic Defence filed with the Registrar an addition to the request. According to the Petkovic Defence, the subjects addressed in the course of its cross-examination of the witness Zelenika were not new subjects and corresponded to what the witness had said in the course of examination-in-chief that was conducted by Mr. Karnavas on the 14th of October, 2008, with regard to document ID 02758. Having examined anew the transcripts of the 14th and 15th of October, 2008, the Chamber notes that Ms. Alaburic covered what the witness had said with regard to document ID 02758 in order to question the witness about the combat of the ABiH in the Konjic region, about the fighting conducted by the ABiH in that region, although the Trial Chamber believes that in the course of the examination-in-chief, the witness's testimony was mainly limited to reading the document, which was described as a combat order. I quote: "The Chamber agrees that it cannot confirm with certainty that Ms. Alaburic actually addressed a new subject..." when referring to the ABiH combat. Given such doubt, the Trial Chamber believes that one should grant the Petkovic Defence's request, and the Trial Chamber, therefore, should not deduct time from the overall amount of time granted. Therefore, the Chamber instructs the Registrar to reallocate the time deducted for the examination of the Zelenika witness. The Chamber notes that a subject referred to in a document that was shown to the witness in the course of examination-in-chief does not authorise a subject to address this subject in the course of the cross-examination properly. In addition, the Chamber informs the parties that when dealing with a new subject in the course of the cross-examination, they should inform the Chamber of the fact. So in two words, the time that was deducted will be reallocated to the overall amount of time granted to the Petkovic Defence; and in the future when you deal with a new subject, inform us of the fact immediately so that we can avoid any problems in the future. That's what our decision was about. Yes, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to greet you, Your Honours, and everyone else in the courtroom; and the Petkovic Defence thanks you for this decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Alaburic. We now have a witness who will be testifying. Mr. Karnavas, no problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No problems, Your Honour. If we could go into private session for, like, 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, we're now in open session. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So in line 13, page 5, "Mr. Khan "should be deleted and replaced with Mr. Karnavas' name. But since Mr. Khan is internationally renowned, it's not surprising. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not nearly as internationally renowned as Mr. Khan, but, in any event, while we're making certain introductions and dealing with matters, while the witness is being brought in, I would like to say that one of our trial attorneys was introduced to the Chamber some months ago. Ms. Hedvig Moe will be taking the cross-examination of this witness. And also, Your Honours, in the course of the testimony of this witness, we expect one of our interns to sit in at least during part of the testimony. She is not here at the moment. She is Laurence Carrier-Desjardins, and we've been pleased to have her as an intern, and as the Chamber knows, we'd like to have the interns in at least once or twice during their internship, and I just wanted to make the Chamber aware of that. And of course, you already know Mr. Bos. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber greets Ms. Hedvig Moe, who is also representing the Prosecution, and it's with pleasure that we'll listen to her cross-examination in the forthcoming days. And naturally, the intern can attend the hearing. She can enter the courtroom as soon as she arrives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I hope all the technical equipment is functioning properly. Could you please give me your first and last name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day. My name is Zdravko Batinic. I was born on the 17th of August, 1955.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a mechanical engineer, and currently I'm involved in security [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, have you already testified before a court with regard to the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read out the solemn declaration that the usher will show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. You may sit down now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to provide you with some information, sir, but I believe that Mr. Karnavas has already provided you with some information in the course of the proofing. First, you will have to answer the questions that Mr. Karnavas will put to you, and Mr. Karnavas will also show you some documents, for sure. After that stage, the Prosecution will conduct its cross-examination. But in the meantime, the Defence teams representing other accused may also intervene in the course of the cross-examination in order to put questions to you once Mr. Karnavas has done so. The Judges who are sitting before you, the four Judges sitting before you, may also put questions to you. This will naturally depend on the documents that you will be shown, and the questions might be put in order to clarify certain issues that are not quite clear. Try and be as precise as possible when answering the questions put to you. If you fail to understand a question, even if a Judge puts a question to you, don't hesitate to ask the person putting the question to you to rephrase that question. Every one and a half hours, we'll have a 20-minute break. As we started at 2.15, the next break will be at 15.45. You have taken an oath, which now means that you're testifying on behalf of justice, and that means you won't have any more contact with Mr. Karnavas right up until the end of your testimony. This is what I wanted to tell you, and naturally the Chamber is at your disposal if necessary if you don't feel well, if you have any questions to put to us. That's what I wanted to tell you, and now I will give the floor to Mr. Karnavas so that he can commence with his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, again, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Mr. Batinic. First, I should correct something on the record. Your current occupation is not in security but, rather, insurance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think that there was a inability to hear what you had indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, before I begin, Your Honours, I should note that there are several documents that we wish to show to the gentleman throughout the course of his testimony that were not initially in our 65 ter list, but we have disclosed them to everyone, and these are 1D 02961, which is the statute of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. This was disclosed last -- about a month ago. Then 1D 03104. These are conclusions from the Gornji Vakuf Municipal Crisis Staff, dated 7 April 1992; 1D 03105, conclusions of the Gornji Vakuf Crisis Staff, this is 15 May 1992; 1D 03106, order of the Gornji Vakuf Municipal Crisis Staff dated 15 May 1992; and then we have some notes from Mr. Batinic's diary. One of them is 1D 03107, an entry of 3 August 1992; another one of 1D 03108, an entry of 14 September 1992; and I'm told that there is -- and that's it, Your Honours. So before I can use these documents, obviously I must seek guidance from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I should also let you know that it was over the weekend that I received these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone in and around the courtroom. The Prosecution objects to the tendering of the diary notes of Mr. Zdravko Batinic. What we've been provided with so far are the excerpts that Mr. Karnavas referred to just now. There is also -- I guess one of those is referenced in the proofing note that we got this afternoon. Two of them are referenced in information that we got on the weekend. Also, we have reason to believe that two other exhibits that have been put on the Prlic 65 ter list previously are from the same diary of Mr. Zdravko Batinic. The Prosecution position is that when certain excerpts of a journal are tendered into evidence or are to be tendered into evidence, then the whole materials, the whole journal, should be disclosed to the Prosecution. I believe a parallel can be drawn to previous Defence witnesses. What comes to mind is Mr. Christopher Beese and Mr. Herbert Okun, Prosecution witnesses, where the Defence position was that the diaries as a whole, respectively, must be disclosed to the Prosecution, and they were at the time. So the Prosecution position is that the whole diary of Mr. Zdravko Batinic should be disclosed. There cannot be only certain excerpts that are picked by counsel that are tendered into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just very briefly, if I may respond. With respect to Mr. Beese, I don't recall that we had -- initially we were going to get everything but, rather, Mr. Beese consented at the end; and the Trial Chamber's position always has been that when it comes to certain diaries, because of the personal nature of them, that some deference is due to the witness in deciding to what extent they will provide portions of the diary. We don't have the entire diary, so it wasn't as if, as is being characterized by the Prosecution, that I picked through the diary. These were sort of during the proofing sessions, the gentleman referred to his diary concerning a particular issue, and based on that, based on his looking into the diary, we made a decision at that point. But we did not get the entire diary ourselves. Otherwise, we would have provided it to the Prosecution, as we did with our previous witness, which I believe was Simunovic. We did provide the entire diary, although we didn't use any of it except on redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber will deliberate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Having deliberated, the Chamber grants the request to have listed on the 65 ter list documents referred to by Mr. Karnavas a minute ago. As far as the schedule is concerned, the diary, rather, the witness's personal diary, the Chamber will give a number for identification of 1D 03108, and we request that the Defence and the witness provide us with the remainder of the diary, with the exception of personal information, personal data. So, Witness, how many pages does your diary consist of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know how many pages exactly. I have two small diaries, and I'm not quite sure how many pages there are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you have a look at your diary this evening, remove personal information or data from the diary - for example, thoughts about your family, things of that kind - and tomorrow you could provide us with the remainder of these diaries. We'll photocopy them, and then Mr. Karnavas could transform this document into a final document. So go through your diary this evening, see what shouldn't be photocopied because it's personal, but everything that concerns political problems, the Gornji Vakuf municipality, everything that seems useful to you could be photocopied tomorrow. And the document was 1D 03108, as I said. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Two points in the matter. Your Honour, first, I don't think it would be meritorious to remove anything from the diary because you would have to cut it. The original should stay as it is. As far as not designating which portions should not be copied, I think that might be a more prudent way of going about it, as opposed to razor-blading pages out. That's number 1. Number 2, I haven't -- you know, I'm prepared at this point to forego those exhibits if the gentleman does not want to disclose the diary. I don't want to seem that we're putting him in a position where he has to turn over something which he doesn't wish to turn over, so -- sorry, if that's -- so I would first want the witness to have that choice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Batinic, you have heard the comments by Mr. Karnavas. It's up to you. Either you believe this to be a personal diary, and then you can tell us, "I prefer to keep it such as it is," and this would then, ipso facto, mean that the two pages or three pages - there are three pages - will not be tendered; or you do not consider it in any way inconvenient and you can put on a piece of paper which pages should not be photocopied because they refer to personal issues. By way of example - I don't know; it's just a hypothesis on my side - let us assume that you have a conversation with your grandmother, and you say that your grandmother is losing her mind or something like that. This is something that we do not have to know. So then you will ask these matters to be extracted from the diary. So my first question is: Do you wish to have it disclosed or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these are my personal notes. I would rather them not be disclosed as a whole. Parts of the diary that I considered could be useful for the Defence are with Mr. Karnavas. As for the rest, I do not wish them to be disclosed to anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, he prefers not to have the diary disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. Well, that's a personal choice that the witness is entitled to make, and we appreciate the Trial Chamber allowing the witness to have that -- make that decision on his own. All right. I should also note one last thing, Your Honour, that we did -- the gentleman did provide us with a map, and that has been disclosed to everyone. We photocopied it. It's not as large, I think, as the original one, but I think it does the trick. We have -- initially, the gentleman did a hand drawing, and we understand he was able to provide us with a map. So with that -- and we will need an IC number for this, for this map, when we get to it, Your Honours. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can we have an IC number for the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, we will see later on for the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Batinic, I understand you are a mechanical engineer by training. Could you please tell us, when did you begin -- when did you finish your studies - on or about, when - and when did you begin working in your profession?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I completed my studies in 19 -- no, I'm sorry, in 1987, and I started working in my profession in mid-May in the springs factory in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, you are originally from Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was born in a locality called Krupa in the municipality of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in that position, working for the springs factory?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: From mid-May 199 -- 1988 - I'm sorry - until the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And why did you stop working at the springs factory?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: By decision of the Municipal Assembly of Gornji Vakuf in December 1991, I was appointed president of the Executive Council of the Municipal Assembly of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And how was it that you were able to be selected to be in that position?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Upon the proposal of the Croatian Democratic Union of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can we then assume that you were a member of the HDZ of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the HDZ of Gornji Vakuf. I still am a member of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when did you become -- when did you initially become a member of HDZ?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of June, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please tell us, at least up until the time that you were appointed to the -- to be the president of the Executive Council of the Municipal Assembly of Gornji Vakuf, what positions did you hold within the HDZ, if any?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Municipal Board of the HDZ for Gornji Vakuf, and I was president of the Executive Board of the branch for a local community in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what about at the state level, the national level?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I was just a member of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now -- and we'll get to some documents about the HDZ. But moving along, if you could please describe to us, very briefly, the functions of the president of the Executive Council of the Municipal Assembly of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The president of the Executive Council of the Assembly of Gornji Vakuf was in charge of coordinating the work of the Executive Council as the government of the Gornji Vakuf municipality. He convenes meetings, assigns decisions and conclusions and opinions of the Executive Council of Gornji Vakuf municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I'm a bit puzzled by the title "Executive Council of the Assembly of the Gornji Vakuf," rather than "Executive Council of the Municipality of Gornji Vakuf." Is that a slip of the tongue, or are these two different things, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, they are not two different things. The Executive Council of the municipality is appointed by the Assembly of the municipality. That's why I'm saying that the Executive Council is a body of the Assembly of the Municipality of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So if I understand your answer correctly, the Executive Council is subordinate to the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And who makes the appointments to the members of the Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The appointments of members of the Executive Council, including the president of the Executive Council, are made by the assembly of the municipality in question, in this case, the Municipality of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if you could please tell us how many members were there in the Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Eight members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please tell us, how were the selections made or the appointments? Who was appointed to those positions? We don't need to know names, but as I understand it, it was on the basis of the political parties.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: By political agreement of the parties with the highest votes after the first multiparty elections in the Municipality of Gornji Vakuf. HDZ was appointed the position of president of the Executive Council, plus three members; and SDA had four members; plus, the SDA was given the position of the president of the assembly of the municipality and the HDZ the, position of the secretary. So all in all, the division was four-four for the two parties, four Croats and four Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you indicated that this was on the basis of the results of the election. Were any positions allocated to SDP, for instance?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And is that -- was there a particular reason?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. The results of the elections, after the 18th of November, 1990, showed that the Assembly of Gornji Vakuf had 50 deputies. 25 seats were won by the SDA, 22 seats by the HDZ, and 3 seats by the SDP of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we go on to your functions and the relationship that the Executive Council had with the Municipal Assembly, if you could tell us whether -- what the system was prior to the first elections. And by that, I mean was there sort of an executive council; was there an assembly before that; and if so, how did it function?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before the multiparty elections, there was a Municipal Assembly of Gornji Vakuf, which had its president and its aldermen, and there was an executive council with its members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And how were the members selected then? Was it based on party line? Was it based on ethnic? Was it some other formula?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: All the members were members of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. I was not a communist, so I don't know how they were selected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, was it -- was there a representation of sorts on the Executive Council to ensure that at least members of the community were represented?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: In Gornji Vakuf, the population consists of Croats and Muslims and very few others, and the communists did make sure that there was ethnic balance before the multiparty elections. So there was ethnic balance in these bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's discuss the executive council that you were in. You indicated that one of your functions was signing conclusions, signing appointments. Were those your decisions or appointments or conclusions?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Those decisions were the decisions of the body of the Executive Council as such. My duty was just to sign the documents or conclusions or appointments made by the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that this was a collective body?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, what was the relationship between the Executive Council and the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The Executive Council of the Assembly was duty-bound to report on its work to the Assembly of Gornji Vakuf, and the Municipal Assembly, in a sense, supervised the work of the Executive Board, assessed the quality of its work. In other words, we were subject to their assessment, to their opinion, and, in the end, to their decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, can you give us an exact date when you took up your position as the president of the Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The first working day in 1992, that is, after the New Year holiday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And for how long or up until what time did you serve in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Until the 11th of January, 1993, inclusive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, very quickly, if we can just -- if you can help us out here. Did the Municipal Assembly continue to work all the way throughout that period?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in a changed form.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what form was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: By decision of the Municipal Assembly of Gornji Vakuf, a crisis staff was formed for the Municipality of Gornji Vakuf on the 7th of April, 1992; and the Assembly, by its decision, transferred all the competences to the Crisis Staff of the municipality. That is the first change. And on the 22nd of June, after a state of war was proclaimed in Bosnia and Herzegovina, all the competencies were passed on to the Council for National Defence or, rather, the Council for National Defence becomes the Presidency of the municipality with all the authority of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you say "Presidency," are we talking about War Presidency, for short?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Many called it "the War Presidency," but officially we called it "the Presidency of the Municipality of Gornji Vakuf."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go back to the Crisis Staff. First, could you please tell us, who were the members of the Crisis Staff now that the Assembly had transferred all of its powers to the Crisis Staff upon its decision?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff of the Municipal of Gornji Vakuf was formed on the 7th of April, 1992, and it consisted of 15 members, 8 Muslims and 7 Croats. The president of the Crisis Staff was the president of the Municipal Assembly, Mr. Mohammed Palic, a Muslim; the deputy president of the Crisis Staff was the president of the Executive Council of the municipality, Zdravko Batinic; and then it also had another 13 members. Among them were presidents of the local boards of the HDZ and the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. These other members, now, you told us they were the presidents of the local boards. Had they been elected to the Assembly? Were they Assembly members that were selected by the Assembly to sit on the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I said, Mr. Karnavas, that among the other 13 were also the president of the HDZ and the SDA, but the members were appointed by the Assembly. So it was upon the proposal of the political parties that a decision was made to appoint members of the Crisis Staff, and that is how there was 8 plus 7 in favour of the Muslims, so a total of 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if I understand you correctly, then, it was the political parties who actually made the selection of who would be on the Crisis Staff, with the exception of the president of the Municipal Assembly and the president of the Executive Council, who were automatically members by virtue of their position. Did I get it right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No, there -- it was not automatic. It was the proposal of the political parties that were part of the government, and the Assembly confirmed their proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But, Mr. Batinic, I just want to make sure I understand you. You mean to tell me the political parties could have removed the president of the Assembly and put somebody else to become the president of the Crisis Staff, or is it that the president of the Assembly and the president of the Executive Council, by virtue of their position, automatically become members of the Crisis Staff, and the others are selected by the respective political parties?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The statute of the Municipal Assembly did not envisage any automatic appointments, and this was the first time in more recent history that such a body was formed. And these 15 members were appointed upon the proposal of the political parties, and it was logical that among them, the president of the Assembly and the president of the Executive Council should be included. That was only logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. How often did the Crisis Staff meet?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: On the day that the Crisis Staff was appointed, it met for the first time in the evening hours and virtually on a daily basis after that or maybe every other day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And was anybody on the Crisis Staff that was from the armed forces, be it from one side or the other or both?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, there were no members of the armed forces on the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, in Gornji Vakuf, was the HVO in existence at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what about -- so this is -- this is 7 April 1992; the HVO did not exist in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: On the 7th of April, 1992, the HVO did not exist in Gornji Vakuf. We had an armed formation. We called it the Municipal Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And who belonged to this Municipal Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The Municipal Staff -- our Municipal Staff was composed of a group of volunteers, mainly reserve officers of the JNA, as an operative staff as of September 1991 and onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you say "we." Who is "we"?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I meant the Croats. The Croats had their operative staff in Gornji Vakuf, the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did the Muslims have something similar?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: They had a crisis staff and groups within that crisis staff, organised through the Patriotic League and the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did there come a time when invitations were extended, be it to the Municipal Staff or to the Patriotic League, to assist in any way the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, could you tell us about when and how?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: At the first meeting of the Crisis Staff for the Municipality of Gornji Vakuf on the 7th of April, in the evening, the Crisis Staff of the HDZ of Gornji Vakuf municipality and of the Crisis Staff of the Patriotic League to propose three operatives, each so that an operative staff for the Municipality of Gornji Vakuf could be formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And did that actually happen? Did it materialise?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you indicated that you met that first night. How often -- well, when it met, did the Crisis Staff have minutes, for instance? Were minutes taken at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And where were these meetings being held?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The meetings of the Crisis Staff for Gornji Vakuf municipality were held in the premises of the president of the Executive Council of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Does that mean that was in your office?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you indicated that at some point, the Crisis Staff becomes the Presidency or War Presidency. That was, I believe you said, June 22nd. Were meetings held then? Did the Presidency hold meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: On the 22nd of June, 1992, after a state of war was proclaimed in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Council for National Defence was transformed into the Presidency of the municipality. That was in accordance with the regulations in force at the time, and each meeting of the Presidency that was held was held in my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And were minutes taken then?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you tell us how many meetings there would have been from, say, June 22nd all the way until the 11th of January, 1993, when you stopped being on the Executive Council or the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: According to my records, there were exactly 16 meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, very briefly, if you could tell us, from the time the Crisis Staff was formed all the way until 11 of January, 1993, were there any incidents in Gornji Vakuf? And if so, I would like to take them chronologically, one by one.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, there were incidents, some of them serious. The first one occurred on the 20th of June, 1992, about noon. There was exchanges of fire in town and the first mortars that were fired from the Muslim part of the town at the Croatian part of the town. The second notable incident occurred in the night between the 24th and 25th of October, and it went on for several days with small lapses, which are due to the behaviour of the commander of the Territorial Defence, Mr. Farudin Agic. Several of their mortar shells exploded in the Croatian part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And was there any --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And was there an incident after that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: After these two mentioned incidents, the next incident -- or it's better to say that that was the beginning of the war between the HVO and the TO, which actually consisted exclusively of Muslims, started on the 11th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And where were you in January 11th, 1993? Could you describe that day, at least, and then we'll work backwards.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: On the 11th of January, 1993, I came to my office, as usual, to work. On that day, I and the new president of the Presidency, Mr. Abdulah Garaca, had a meeting with the European Monitors in his office. After that, I went home for lunch; and after that, I don't know how, but the conflict started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And after the conflict started, how long did it last?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: With more or less intensity, as long as the snipers were active, this conflict came to an end on the 24th of February, 1993, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. You'll need to speak a little slower so we can get the full translation. Okay. Now, just a couple of matters that I want to touch on. First of all, were you a member of the HVO - and I'm talking about the military, you know - were you a soldier prior to the 11th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you ever become a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At what point in time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of January, 1996, I -- 1993, I joined the volunteer forces of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That was the 13th of January?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: I voluntarily joined the HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was on the 13th, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And we can talk about that at some point, but what about the HVO Gornji Vakuf, the civilian authorities? Were you a member of the HVO Gornji Vakuf at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: If you're talking about the HVO as executive government, Zdravko Batinic wasn't a member of that body in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Here you could say that you weren't, but -- all right. Now, did it exist -- did the HVO, this executive government, if you will, did it exist in Gornji Vakuf? And if so, could you please describe to us how it existed ?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: In Gornji Vakuf, the HVO government body, administrative body, existed on paper. It had a president and three or four individuals who were appointed by the decision of the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Mate Boban, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, did this executive authority, this HVO Gornji Vakuf, ever attempt to take over the Executive Council or the Crisis Staff of the Presidency? Did it make any moves, political or military, to take over those authorities?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: To your understanding, did the HVO Gornji Vakuf have a police force?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did it pass decisions on administrative matters, such as taxation?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you ever participate in any meetings that were being held by members of the HVO Gornji Vakuf? And if so, could you please describe them to us?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was invited to a number of meetings of the HVO as a member of the executive authority, as the most responsible person working in the municipal bodies of power, on behalf of the Croatian people, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, who was the president of the HVO Gornji Vakuf, this executive authority?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The president was Mr. Ivan Saric, the president of the HVO civil authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did he hold another position at the time as well?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He was the president of the Municipal Board of the HDZ for the Gornji Vakuf municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked to speak a little more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm asked that you -- if you could speak a little slower, it would be most helpful, and maybe enunciate. They're having a hard time. Was Mr. Saric at the time a -- or you were a member of the Presidency at the time, correct, when you were attending these meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about Mr. Saric? Was he also a member of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ivan Saric was a member of the Crisis Staff of the Gornji Vakuf municipality, and he was a member of the Presidency for the Gornji Vakuf municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did Mr. Saric at any point in time try to impose the will, his will or the will of HVO Gornji Vakuf, this executive authority, upon that of the Crisis Staff or the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go back to these incidents that we spoke of. You told us that the first incident happened on or about June 1992. Can you tell us, who was responsible, in your opinion, if you know, for that incident?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the person responsible for the first armed clash in Gornji Vakuf was Hanefija Prijic, also known as Paraga. He was a commander of the Green Beret unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Was this Green Beret unit also participating or assisting in any way the Crisis Staff at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: All armed formations in the area of Gornji Vakuf were considered by the Crisis Staff of Gornji Vakuf to be legitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So are you saying -- well, was the HVO considered legitimate?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was the Patriotic League considered legitimate?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: As part of the Territorial Defence, they were considered to be legitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what about these Green Berets under this fellow named Paraga or aka Paraga?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I think that the Green Beret unit was founded and armed by the Patriotic League, and they were directly linked to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was he from the area?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was born in a settlement called Voljice in the Municipality of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, were there any units from Croatia there, HV units?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were there any individuals there who had come from Croatia and were participating in any armed force activity?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And who were they?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: They were members of the Croatian people who had gone to war as volunteers to the Republic of Croatia. This was when there was Serbian aggression carried out against the Republic of Croatia. And after the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina broke out, many of them, almost all of them, came to the territory in which they had grown up or to the territory that their parents were from, so there was a significant number of Croats from the Municipality of Gornji Vakuf. And as members of the Croatian Army, they were in the Croatian Army, and then they went to Gornji Vakuf and joined the units of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. When --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm just asking for the time period here to be specified. The witness -- the witness is talking about HV members, and I'd like to know more about when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When did these folks arrive?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: They started arriving at the beginning of April 1992. They started to arrive in our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Was there a particular unit; and if so, did it have a name; and if so, what was it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I don't know that there was a particular unit that had only such members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was anyone in particular who was in charge, a commander?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, after the events in June, on June 20th, could you please describe to us the atmosphere in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult to explain this when there are two friendly peoples who are involved in an armed conflict for the first time. There is fear, suspicion, a lack of trust. This escalates. This is something that had never happened before. This happened on the 26th [as interpreted], and then there was fear, a lack of understanding. It's very difficult to explain such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you say it happened on the 26th, when it happened on the 26th, which day -- which month are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The 26th [as interpreted] of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was it -- I'm told that it's 20th --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: 20th, the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So I would ask you to please enunciate to make sure that we have a correct record. So -- all right. Now, were check-points put up in Gornji Vakuf, and if so, by whom?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Check-points at the entrance and exit in Gornji Vakuf were set up at three places: One in the direction of Gornji Vakuf to Prozor, one in the direction of Gornji Vakuf in the direction of Bugojno, and one in the direction of Gornji Vakuf towards Novi Travnik. At these check-points, there were members of the HVO and of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. At that point in time, can you tell us whether the HVO and the Territorial Defence were getting along? Were they cooperating, coordinating?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. To what extent?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: After the HVO had lost Kupres, units of the HVO from the Gornji Vakuf municipality held the defence line at the Radisa Mountain in the direction of Kupres. After a certain amount of time, the HVO units were joined by Territorial Defence units at the same line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The clock should stop because now I'm waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking for time specifics, again, both on the check-points that were mentioned and also on this last portion on Kupres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What month are we talking about, because I thought we were still on June 20th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The check-points that were held by the HVO and the Territorial Defence were held from the beginning of April 1992. This was at the entrance to Gornji Vakuf municipality and at the exit from that municipality. Their cooperation at the defence lines in the direction of Kupres was from May until the beginning of the January conflict in 1993. These were the defence lines facing the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. What year -- this is until the conflict of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, after the June incident, did those check-points continue to exist, the same ones, or did -- were there additional ones?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: There were no additional check-points. When a day or two later the situation had become more stable, the forces of the HVO and Territorial Defence were at the same check-points again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, did the Presidency ever make any efforts to find out what exactly happened on June 20th, or 18th, 19th, 20th, those days?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The Presidency of the Gornji Vakuf municipality issued an order requesting that an investigation be launched by the authorised organs of the HVO and the Territorial Defence and the police station. They were to investigate the reasons for which this incident had occurred on the 20th of June, 1992. They were to determine who was responsible and who started it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And was that resolved? Did they ever come up with a report?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. They forwarded their reports to us as the Presidency of the Municipality, a report which was written, and they said they weren't fully in agreement with regard to the character of that incident, with regard to the perpetrators or those who had started the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, the next incident that occurred around the 24th /25th of October, could you please tell us what happened then, and for how long did it last?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I have to go back two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, go for it.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Okay. On the 19th of June -- I apologise. On the 19th of October, 1992, there was some kind of an incident in Novi Travnik. In a certain way, it increased tension in the territory of our municipality too. On the 19th, the 20th, and the 21st and the 22nd, 23rd and 24th of October, the structure of the civilian authorities in the Municipality of Gornji Vakuf, the representatives of the HVO and the Territorial Defence attempted to have daily meetings. Sometimes they had two meetings a day, and they also had a peace march through the town. And they did all this in order to prevent incidents from breaking out in our municipality. But between the 24th and 25th, unfortunately, things got out of hand. Some shells were launched by the Territorial Defence on the Croatian part of Gornji Vakuf; and as a result, a conflict between the HVO and the Territorial Defence broke out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is once against kindly asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm being told to tell you to slow down, so please slow down, enunciate, because it's very important that we get the full translation. Did you participate in the peace march?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, after this incident or incidents, did the Presidency or members of the Presidency hold a meeting to find out what had happened, who did what to whom and why?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were there any meetings held at the end of October concerning this?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please describe them?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of October, 1992, in the old hotel, we held the first meeting of the representatives of the Croats and of the Muslims. At that meeting -- well, that meeting was attended by the most important representatives of the Muslims and the Croats. There were commanders of armed units who also attended, commanders of the HVO and of the TO, the Territorial Defence. On the following day, on the 31st of October, a similar body met, and the purpose of this meeting was to try and calm the situation down, to return to some kind of a normal life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, at that meeting, did you learn who had been responsible for starting the incident back on the 24th of October, 24th/25th?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: There were various assessments made. However, Farudin Agic gave a statement, which was put in such a way that he, in fact, indirectly admitted that the forces of the Territorial Defence had started the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you recall, could you please describe in greater detail what exactly Mr. Agic said that led you to believe that it was the forces of the Territorial Defence that had started this conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Three or four days that preceded the 24th of October, 1992, well, in the light of the conversations of the Croatian and Muslim leadership, we tried to avoid incidents of any kind through these conversations. We promised each other that TO units and HVO units would not be used against Croats or Muslims. We promised each other not a single Command of the HVO and TO would send any units outside the area of Gornji Vakuf. In other words, we tried to guarantee for each other that such a conflict wouldn't break out. However, on the meeting held on the 30th of October, 1992, Mr. Agic said quite precisely, contrary to our agreement, a company from Priboj [as interpreted] as been sent out, which together with Muslims forces from Hara [phoen] attacked the HVO at the Medik [phoen] elevation. He added that the situation was out of control, and then individual commanders willfully took a decision, lost their nerves, and launched a few shells on the Croatian part of town. They destroyed some routes on the Prozor-Gornji Vakuf road. This was a direct admission of how the conflict in Gornji Vakuf had broken out on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that the next incident began on or about 11 January 1993, and before we discuss that incident, can you please tell us what the situation was like in Gornji Vakuf, say, at the end of October, beginning of November, all the way until January 11th, when the next conflict began?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: From the beginning of November 1992 up until the end of 1992, things became more normal, although there was a lot of distrust, an incredible amount of distrust. However, nothing happened that would make one think that we could expect some kind of a new incident in the future. However, in the period from Christmas up until the 25th of December, until the 6th of January, in fact, 1993, there were incidents which broke out because the Muslim representatives who would remove Croatian symbols, insignia, that Croats would put up for Christmas and the new year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We're going to get to that when we look at some of the documents, but let me just get a little ahead of myself because we do have a document saying that flags of either side were not to be displayed, and now you're telling us here that Croatian symbols and insignia were being displayed around Christmas and New Year's. Can you explain that? If there was a decision not to have those displays, how was it that they went up around Christmas and New Year?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The definite decision that you are referring to had to do with the period from the 24th of June, 1992, and the purpose was to calm down the situation after the first incident that broke out in Gornji Vakuf on the 20th of June, 1992. However, for Christmas and the New Year, Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina traditionally put out their national symbols. In this case, the Croatian flag in Bosnia-Herzegovina had been put up at a few sites in town. This irritated someone, and then Muslims and members of the armed forces and of the Territorial Defence took those flags down on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, first, a point of clarification. You said the Croatian flag, and some of us may think that this is the flag of the Republic of Croatia. Is that what we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No, no. I said the flag of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which has a different coat of arms from the coat of arms that you see on the flag of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, prior to this incident, prior to Christmas, were there any Muslim holidays? And if so, did the Muslims in Gornji Vakuf display their symbols, their flag or what have you, in celebration of their religious holiday?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. On that year [as interpreted] before Christmas, the Muslims celebrated Bajram or Gurban Bajram to be more precise, and there were flags and symbols that they had put up in town. There was the green flag with a half moon and the flag with the lilies, and no one touched them. No one took them down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I believe it's time for the break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's quarter to 4.00, and we will have our technical 20-minute break. We will resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Batinic, we left off around 11 January 1993. If you could briefly just tell us, to the best of your knowledge, what happened on that day. I know that you went to work, you went to your office, and I believe you indicated that later on that afternoon is when the conflict broke out. Could you tell us, to your understanding, what exactly occurred?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I have to say that I don't know what exactly happened or how the conflict started on the 11th of January, 1993, in Gornji Vakuf, so I just don't have enough information or knowledge to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you indicated that at some point, you did join the HVO. Could you tell us about what time that was, what period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of January, 1993, in the evening, I was in a house, which was about 150 metres away from my house and where the Command of the HVO was situated to defend the part of the town inhabited by Croats. According to information conveyed to me and which were not at all good for the HVO, there was a danger of the breakthrough of the Muslim forces into the Croatian part of the town. In view of the fact that my house [as interpreted] and my family [as interpreted], inhabited by my small children and my wife, was only some 150 metres away from the separation line, I voluntarily placed myself at the service of the HVO, put on a uniform, picked up a rifle, and became a member of the HVO armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps it may be a good time at this point to look at the map that you provided us; and so we could just very briefly inform the Trial Chamber, I will not ask you anything in detail. Others can. They may have more time to do so, but I -- perhaps if we could put it on the ELMO, and you could help us out here a little bit. I don't know if that's helpful for the Trial Chamber, but at least can you tell us -- all right. First of all, where did you get this map from?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I got this map as chief of Uskoplje municipality in the period of 1996 from a member of the peace-keeping forces stationed in the territory of Gornji Vakuf Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to need you to mark some areas on this map, so I'm going to need to have you -- do you have a pen that's handy? Otherwise, I can provide you with something. The gentleman behind you will provide you with a magic marker. Mr. Batinic, you're going to need to mark the map itself. All right? If you could please first describe what it is that we're seeing.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: We are seeing a map of Gornji Vakuf, the urban part of the Municipality of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where your offices were located, where the Executive Council met?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The municipality building was here [indicating].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Just put an "M" there. Okay. Could you mark it with an "M", please, because later on we will not be able to determine what marking signifies what.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, where was your house at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: [Indicates] Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Could you put an "H" there for "House"?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Eventually, there was a confrontation line, as I understand it, in Gornji Vakuf. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please draw that? Where was the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And you might want to put a "C" there so we know later on that this is the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where you were stationed or where you were located when you were serving in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, were you there the entire time in that location?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: For the first ten days, from the 13th of January until the 23rd or 24th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Why don't you put a "1," then. Put a "1" next to the line so we know that this line signifies where you were initially.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And after that, where did you move to? What location?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: To the so-called industrial zone. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And where were you exactly located?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: [Indicating]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Maybe you could put a "2" around that circle so we know you that were located there.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And perhaps you can tell us why you moved from your initial position, designated as "1," to the industrial zone, which is designated as "2." What was the reason?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: When the forces of the HVO gained control of a strategic quarter above the town of Gornji Vakuf - we called it the relay, which was here [indicates] - then there was no longer any danger of the Muslim forces passing through Glavica here [indicates] attacking the settlement here [indicates], which was originally Croatian, and that is why the decision was made --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here, because we have to go step by step, because saying "here" and "there" later on, on the transcript, is not going to be very helpful. So we have to designate it on the map itself.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So why don't you tell us where the HVO was. Can you put "HVO" in the locations where they were located? And then we'll do the same thing with the TO.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The HVO was situated in this part of town [indicates], from the -- left of the confrontation line. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And put "HVO" because you have an "H" already there.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And where were the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Right of the separation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Put down "TO." All right.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: And here, too. [Indicates] [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What's that second part where you have the "TO" again, the second TO? What is that location?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: An elevation point above the town of Gornji Vakuf where the TV relay station was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And is that a significant location? And if so, why?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: From this position, one controls the entire territory of the town. With fire from firearms, one could hit virtually anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me go back to my initial question. You indicated that you moved from location 1 to location 2, the industrial zone. Why did you move there? What was there that made you and others, I suspect, move to that location?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: After a unit that was stationed in the industrial zone at the beginning of the conflict had left, this area was left undefended by the HVO. And since all Croatian-inhabited areas were behind the industrial zone, it was necessary to protect this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you say "this area," we're talking about the area that you circled, or is there more area than the one that is encircled?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: From the road leading from Gornji Vakuf towards Bugojno passing along the industrial zone, all the settlements behind that industrial zone, which cannot be seen on this map, were inhabited by Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Why don't you draw an arrow so at least we know exactly where the Croats are inhabited. Draw an arrow in the direction which they are located. Perhaps we could give the gentleman -- I'm sure the Tribunal could afford something more robust than the magic marker that we've handed him.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you could please tell us, how long were you in that location, number 2?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Until the 24th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Who else was there with you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: There was a group of Domobrans, as we call them, of some 20 men, among them the former president of the Basic Court in Bugojno, teachers, engineers, older people who were from this part -- of our part of town who were not in other units of the HVO, in other words, the Home Guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you indicated that that conflict began on or about 11 January 1993, and it went all the way until, I believe you said, the 24th of February, 1993. You've indicated to us that there was a separation line that we can see that you have drawn and designated as "C." Can you please tell us at what point in time the separation line went away.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: At the end of February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So after 1993, there was no separation line; everybody went back? Everybody could move around Gornji Vakuf as before?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Quite so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I have no further questions at this time regarding this map. If the Trial Chamber wishes to ask any questions ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, a small technical question. On the map, you have indicated the positions of the Territorial Defence of the Muslims, I assume, the TO. At the time, was it not the BiH army rather than the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know exactly when the TO or the army of the Muslim people proclaimed themselves to be the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is why I called them the TO, because it was exclusively composed of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And what was the name of their leader?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume the commander of the TO Staff was the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But what was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fahrudin Agic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, during that time that you were an active soldier, did you ever have enemy contact? Did you ever have within shooting range an enemy, someone from the TO, as you call it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the lines that we held as defence, we were all exposed to small-fire arms. To small-arms fire, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I can understand that, but did any enemy soldier come near? Did you ever have to reject an attack, actually, enemy movement, or was it more a static situation such as we have reports from periods during World War I?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the defence line that I was at, there were no attempts by the Muslim forces to break through physically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You want a number for this document, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar, can we have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be given Exhibit number IC 00878. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, before we leave -- before we leave this, just a couple of technical questions. You showed us where your house was. On January 11th when you went to work, did you know or did you expect that something was about to happen that particular day?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know whether anything was planned, pre-planned?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, of course you weren't a member of the HVO, the military component. Who was the commander of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The commander of the HVO in Gornji Vakuf was Mr. Zrinko Tokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe he has to sign the document, although I don't -- technically, I don't think it's necessary, although somehow it's become a tradition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not obligatory, but it's always better to do more than not enough, so please sign the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could sign the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And maybe put a date on it, too, so we know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could date it also, Mr. Batinic. It's the 10th, I believe, 10/11.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tokic, did you know him at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew Mr. Tokic very well, and I can say that at the time, he was a friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And by the way, your offices, what side of town were they located?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The building of the Municipal Assembly and my office were in the part of town inhabited 90 per cent by Muslims in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm going to need the assistance of the usher to give you your documents, and we're going to start going through them in a rather quick pace, and you can turn to the first document. It's 1D 02699, 1D 02699. Do you recognise the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what is it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: This is the first statute of the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina passed at the founding assembly in Sarajevo on the 18th of August, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether you had attended that particular assembly? You did indicate to us that you were a member of HDZ.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I was present at the founding meeting as an envoy of the HDZ for Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So I take it you are familiar with this particular statute.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, perhaps you could help us out here a little bit because one of the central issues here is, of course, what was the HDZ, what was its principles; and of course, later on that ties into the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So if I could get you to look at Article 4, for instance, in this document. Article 4, do you have it, sir? It may be easier if you just look at the hard copy. All right. Now, in Article 4, it says here that the BH HDZ shall be active in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then it goes on to talk about that the BH HDZ is a constitutive part of the united HDZ organisation whose seat is in Zagreb. Could you please tell us, what did that mean, keeping in mind that this is 18 August 1990.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina was considered a constituent part of the planet-wide organisation of the Croatian Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At that period in time, 18 August 1990, was Croatia an independent nation?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it the same goes with the -- with Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you still had a Yugoslavia intact?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what happened once the Republic of Croatia became independent, as did the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?
