utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The HDZ for Bosnia and Herzegovina was an autonomous political organisation, active exclusively within the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we go to page 16 of the English document, and I believe you might have it marked. I don't know exactly what page it is for you, but it's titled "Programme Declaration of the Founding Assembly of the Croatian Democratic Union of BH." Do you have that located, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we look at this, look at Roman numeral III. Perhaps you can help us out here. It says here: "In accordance with these starting points and opinions," the ones that are referred to in 1 and 2, "the HDZ BH will focus on establishing the constitutional and legal order of the original parliamentary pluralistic democracy. Implementation of this order must be founded on consistent adherence, without exception, to the general human rights declaration, which was proclaimed 10 December 1948." And then if we go all the way down to, for instance, A, B and C, we see -- in particular, what interests me is number C: "Diversity is inherent to a pluralist society, so the HDZ BH, too, is pluralist in all its constituent and working elements." What does that mean? Can you help us out?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: This means that we, as a political party in Bosnia-Herzegovina, advocated a pluralist society, a multiethnic state, for equal rights of all three nations in Bosnia and Herzegovina, for equal rights of all constituent peoples, that is, the Croats, Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we could go on to the next document, 1D 02798. I won't ask you any questions concerning what is a constituent nation or peoples. Others may wish to ask. I think that topic has been discussed at length throughout the last three years in this case. Do you have the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If I could focus your attention to the lower part of the first page where it says "Here..." -- well, first, let me ask you, do you recognise this document? It says: "Election declaration of the people of Gornji Vakuf Municipality." Do you recognise the document?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at the last page or the end of this document, we do not see a date. We see a reference in the very first paragraph, but we don't see a date at the end. Do you know -- do you have any idea on or about when this document was made?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The election declaration to the inhabitants of Gornji Vakuf by the Municipal Board of the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina was issued by the Municipal Board of the HDZ of Gornji Vakuf prior to the first multiparty elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, on the eve of those elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And, of course, you have seen this document before, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In fact, how is it that I have it to show it to you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: All members of the Municipal Board of the HDZ of Gornji Vakuf took part in the drafting of this document, which means I was also a participant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But how did I get a hold of it? That's my question. I'm trying to lay a foundation without leading.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I gave you this document from my own archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, if we look at the -- if we focus our attention towards the latter part of the first page, it says: "Here are the basic principles of our election platform: By voting for the HDZ, you will vote for ..." And it talks about irrefutable sovereignty of BiH, equality of the Croatian people as a constituent and state-building nation of BiH. You then go on -- it then goes on to talk about economic, trait -- spiritual and cultural ties with -- between BH, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia and Europe, since they constitute a single entity. And then it goes on to say: "... transformation of BiH into a confederative, democratic, multiparty and parliamentary state founded on the respect of human rights and freedoms of all citizens who enjoy the same status and equality, regardless of their nationality, religion or belief." Could you please tell us, what exactly is this document talking about, since you participated in this process at the time this document was generated?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: By this document, the Municipal Board of the HDZ of Gornji Vakuf sent a message to their voters and calling them to vote and indicating what the HDZ of Gornji Vakuf would be advocating and, generally speaking, the whole HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina, of course, after the elections are completed and once we take part in the bodies of authority in the municipality and the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If you go on to the second page, there are two items that I'm sure may have piqued someone's interest in and around this courtroom. This would be the same page for you. It talks about: "Put an end to demographic discontent; a democratic revival of the Croatian ethnic being -- putting to an end to the departure and a speedy and full return of the Croats who have moved away." What is meant by "to put an end to demographic discontent"? Some may think that this has something to do with ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I object to leading, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't know how this is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, rephrase your question in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In general terms. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What is meant by "demographic discontent"?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Before the first multiparty elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, given political persecution, unemployment and certain other reasons, the Croats emigrated from Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was perhaps for political reasons or because they couldn't find work in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this has to do with demographic discontent, above all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then if we go further down, it talks about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas. I would like to understand what is meant by "demographic discontent," and I must confess that so far I've heard that people left because of the economic situation, and I cannot link that to the term "demographic discontent." So if you could try to explain this term, I would be grateful, Mr. Puntic [sic].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A significant number of Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina had to leave Bosnia and Herzegovina for political reasons. A significant number of Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina had to go after bread outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina because at the time, at the time of the communist period, there was discrimination when it came to employing Croatians. So this demographic content mostly had to do with this: Demographic renewal assumed that in a new Bosnia and Herzegovina, in a multiparty Bosnia-Herzegovina, the state would take care of young families. They would provide incentives. When it came to accommodation, they'd give them family leave -- give them maternity leave that would last for one year, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, in more conventional language, what you mean by "demographic discontent," others would call "discrimination on ethical grounds." Is that what you're actually saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me -- let me perhaps add a couple of questions to this one. You indicated that the Croatian peoples were one of the constituent nations in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Muslims and the Serbs being the other two. Can you tell us, what was the percentage of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina among the population?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: According to the census of 1991, in Bosnia-Herzegovina there were 17.3 per cent of Croats out of the total number of the population, 17.3 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, is there a distinction between being a constituent nation and a national minority? And if so, could you please tell us what that distinction is?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: A constituent nation in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- well, the constituent nations were the Croats, the Serbs and the Muslims; and they were, in fact, the bearers of the statehood of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And as a constituent people, any one of those three peoples mentioned had the right to expect that they could participate in government, that government would be shared between the constituent peoples in an equal manner. National minorities could not expect or count on being included in this division of power, in sharing in government, and that's the significant distinction that has to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And did that exist prior to the first free elections?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, but as to what extent, when it comes to the Croatian people -- well, at the time I hadn't spent much time in Bosnia and Herzegovina, so I could not really say, but I do know that people were unhappy with the way in which they were represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, does there come a point where, with the percentage, if it drops to a certain point -- you have 17.3, 1991 census. If that percentage drops, is there the possibility that the Croats or any constituent nation might lose its status as a constituent nation and become a minority -- a national minority?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the critical threshold is in terms of the percentage of the population or, rather, of a given people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but this should never happen in any event, since we're talking about constituent peoples here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. One last item on this document. Towards the end of the page, it talks about the obligation of the existing system of teaching alphabets and that the Latin alphabet, in the Croatian language, should be used in the textbooks. Could you please explain to us, why was this in the platform?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: In this way, we were demanding that the Latin script be used in schools and that our children in schools learn the Croatian language. We wanted educational programmes to be in the Croatian language for our children. We did not dispute the right that other peoples or, rather, the other peoples had to organise the educational system as they desired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to the next document, 1D 02579.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we go on to the following document: Witness, I've just had a look at the last document, 2798, and I compared it to the first document, 2698. The second document was adopted the 22nd of September, a few days later, and the first document was adopted on the 18th of August. And when we have a look at the two documents, we have the impression that the second follows on immediately from the first document. In the first document, Article 10 states quite explicitly that the HDZ is fighting to be included in the European Union. In the second document, we have something to the same effect. This is 1990. At the time, Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina had not yet been recognised as independent republics. At the time, we still had the ancient -- the old communist system. Since very explicit reference is made to the European Union, would you say that there was a general consensus, at least at the level of the HDZ, when it came to this idea of joining the European Union? What would your opinion be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All those who became members of the HDZ and accepted the HDZ programme and its principles agreed with what is stated under Article 10 of the first statute of the BH statute, and they also agreed with everything that was in the declaration of their programme. So the statute was accepted, and the principles according to which the party should operate were also accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When we see these two documents and the role that the Croats had to play in the future, I wonder why the Gornji Vakuf HDZ at the election held on the 22nd of September, 1990, mentions the Croatian people; but you speak about Bosnia and Herzegovina and about Croatia. Weren't there any Croats in Serbia? What happened to the Croats from Serbia? Why is there no reference to the Croats in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd just like to correct something. This document mentions or refers to document 798. It mentions the 22nd of September, 1990, which is when there was an electoral assembly of the municipal organisation of HDZ for the Gornji Vakuf municipality, and this document was drafted later on, just before the first multiparty elections held in Bosnia and Herzegovina; in other words, at the beginning of November, 1990. This document had to be based on the statute of the HDZ in Bosnia and Herzegovina and on the principles contained in the programme of the HDZ in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in a certain sense. And when we talk about economic, spiritual and civilization matters, well, in a certain way we are confirming our roots in Europe. We always believe that we, in some sense, belong to the West.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you haven't answered my question. Why did one deliberately leave out the Croats in Serbia? Why is there no reference made to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are an organisation that is active in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next document, 1D 02579. 1D 02579. We see this is the political charter of the HDZ BH, and if we look at the end of this document, we see "Mostar, November 1992." And it's signed by the HDZ Central Committee Chairman Mate Boban. Were you aware of this document, sir, at the time when it was generated?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I saw it after it was drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you provided me with this document, as well, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at paragraph number 3 -- Roman numeral III, again, we see that the Croatian Democratic Union is in favour of immediate cessation of war in BH and for the internal structure of BH based on the following principles: "1. BH is a sovereign, independent and internationally-recognised state; "2: BH comprises three constitutional and equal nations, the Croats, the Muslims and the Serbs; "3. HDZ BH is in favour of internal structure based on the principles established with the European Community and agreement reached between Tudjman and Izetbegovic." And then it goes on to say: "Croatian Democratic Union is in favour of BH as a state of three constitutive units as the only solution that will guarantee all the civil and national rights of the Croats." If you could please explain that to us. What is meant by this, and why the reference to Tudjman and Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The HDZ in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Croatian Democratic Party, from the time it was founded up until the very present day was in favour of an independent and integral Bosnia and Herzegovina as stated in this charter, but the structure was to be different from the structure envisaged by others. The structure was to be such that the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina would also be content. Three constituent peoples had the right to have equal rights in Bosnia-Herzegovina; and when reference is made to the Tudjman-Izetbegovic agreement, the Agreement on Friendship and Cooperation from July is what they have in mind, July 1992, when reference was made to the constituent units in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to the next document, which is -- it's 1D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a follow-up question. Here, again, I have the same concern I expressed a minute ago with regard to the Croats from Serbia. In this document, which is an important one because it's been signed by Mr. Boban - he signed it in November 1992 - in this document, in paragraph 3, reference is made to the three constituent peoples, the Serbs, the Croats and the Muslims, but no reference is ever made to Milosevic. Reference is made to Tudjman and Izetbegovic, and it seems that one is leaving aside the Serbian issue, whereas the Serbian issue was at the heart of the problems in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this is what we came to see later on in the form of Republika Srpska. You exercised political power, so how would you explain this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when this political charter was drafted, Bosnia and Herzegovina was an independent and internationally-recognised state, and this charter explicitly refers to the agreement signed by President Izetbegovic, as president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, together with the president of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Tudjman. They're referred to because these two presidents agreed on certain positions that had to do with the internal structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina; and given that at the same time a similar agreement had not been signed with the president of Serbia, Mr. Milosevic, it was not possible to make reference to this issue in the charter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: A couple of follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At that point in time in history, was the entire BiH a free territory?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: It depends on your perspective. In our opinion, it wasn't. For the Croats and Muslims, the entire of Bosnia-Herzegovina was not free.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. What had the Serbs or the SDA -- the SDS, what had they done prior to the -- to Bosnia-Herzegovina being declared independent, prior to the referendum?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I know that prior to the referendum on an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the 28th and 29th of February, 1992, some kind of economic communities had been established or, rather, they'd already - roughly speaking - defined the area to be covered by Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Unless there are any other questions, I'll move on. If we go on now to the next document, 1D 02700, now we're into 17 December 1993. Again, this is a statute of the Democratic Union. Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I want to focus your attention to paragraph 10 -- to Article 10, I should say. That would be on page -- bottom of page 2, top of page 3 in English. And in particular, again, for continuity's sake, to see how the HDZ is progressing, how their platform is moving, 10.1, it talks about to ensure the rights of the Croatian people, self-determination, statehood, independence, sovereignty. So you see that, sir, right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it also talks about -- that Bosnia-Herzegovina consists of three equal constitutive nations: Croats, Muslims and Serbs. You see that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then if we go to 10.2, it talks about: "... to further the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna as a democratic parliamentary multiparty state that shall guarantee and ensure all constitutional rights and liberties to each of its constituent nations and to every citizen, irrespective of race, nationality, religion, political persuasion, gender, or social status." Now, I want to focus your attention to the word "state," because if we look at paragraph 10.1, it talks about Bosnia-Herzegovina, and now here we see that the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna talks about a multiparty state. Can you please help us out here?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. This statute was adopted in December 1993, and it confirms the continuity of the policies pursued by the HDZ in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Its policies were for Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent and integral state, but it was in favour of a Bosnia and Herzegovina that had an internal structure that was also suited to the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina. At that time, there was the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, which in the opinion of the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina was to be an integral part of the state of Bosnia -- of the states of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Unless there are other questions, I'm going to move on for the sake of time, although I do point out, at least for the record, 10.4, that's for Judge Trechsel, given the earlier question regarding demographic discontent. That may be of some interest. Otherwise, I'll move on. The next document is 1D 02580, and do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I don't see at the end of the document a date or a signature, but do you know where this document came from?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: This is a political declaration from the HDZ in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Although I'm not sure, I believe that it was drafted just before this assembly, or perhaps it was adopted at the assembly on the 17th of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we can see from the very first paragraph it talks about the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and so that would at least help us out here and -- as to what months and thereafter this document would have been generated. But let me focus your attention on Roman numeral I, the third paragraph - that's on the first page for us in the English - because it talks about the HDZ BiH is campaigning for a democratically-organised Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna which guarantees and ensures all rights and freedoms to each of its citizens, regardless of race, nationality, sex, religious views, political convictions, or social status. It then goes on to talk about preconditions of halting the exodus of Croats and ensuring the return of expellees, refugees and displaced persons. Now, sir, could you please help us out here. At that point in time, since you were a member of HDZ, what were the aspirations of HDZ, and are they accurately reflected in this political declaration?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The aspirations of the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina were expressed very frankly in this political declaration. In certain areas inhabited by Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croats felt more threatened than most of the Croats who lived in the territory of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and that's why it is explicitly stated here that the HDZ will take care of Croats throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on now to the next document, 1D 027 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If you allow, Mr. Karnavas, I would like to ask a question in this context, but it's a bit more general, perhaps, in nature. Mr. Buntic [sic] --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Batinic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, I'm sorry, was the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna a multiethnic state? What was the position of Muslims in Herceg-Bosna? Were they a constituent nation, or were they rather a minority, if you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna did not have its border area. We had an area where many Croats lived, and we called it the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. In that area, there were Muslims, as well, and the Muslims a constituent people in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe we'll be hearing more about this in the course of the evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I also would like to ask a follow-up question here as regards to that statute. Statute, yes. In Article 4 of the general provisions, and the second part of that Article 4, it is the following, and I quote: "HDZ BH shall be an integral part of the overall HDZ organisation, with seat located in Zagreb." Now, my question is how Mr. Batinic would interpret this particular sentence and this Article 4, since then the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, HDZ BH, had its seat located in Sarajevo; and now here in Article 4, that is that reference which I quoted, that that very organisation shall be an integral part of the overall HDZ organisation, that is, that one which was created and which was functioning in the Croatian Republic. So I wonder what kind of explanation is to be given by Mr. Batinic in terms of the independence of the HDZ BH or if there was any kind of dependency, being dependent upon the centre which was located in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, you need to look at the very first document that was introduced. That was 1D 02699, dated 18 August 1990. We were now in 1993, but I believe the question goes to this particular document, Article 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: With due respect, Mr. Karnavas, I think it refers to the document 1D 02700. At least, there in Article 4 we have this reference to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I wasn't sure which document we were referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Prandler should actually -- 2700?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you. I refer to the same document which was before us, that is, the statute in Croatia which says Hrvatska Demokratska Zajednica, and the statute, Mostar, 17. procinca, in 1993. So it is what I am -- what I quoted, actually, in the Croatian language -- [Interpretation] Article 4. [In English] It is what I quoted, the second part of Article 4, so that one which I asked if there was any kind of, quote/unquote, "dependency"; of the HDZ upon the centre and the leadership, quote/unquote, "in Zagreb."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina operated autonomously in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Globally viewed, the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina coordinated its activities with the HDZ in Croatia. At the beginning when it was founded and for several years after that, we considered ourselves to be a component of the planet-wide HDZ, as the HDZ had its branches in Europe, America, Australia and so on. To be more precise in interpreting this statute, I cannot be, as in each of our statutes, including this one, it says that the authentic interpretation of this statute can be given by the Presidency of the HDZ for BiH, that is, the Presidency at the time, or the commission for statutes authorised by the Presidency and the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Well, frankly, I am not truly convinced by the answer, but I leave it as it is, and I believe that there are certain question marks still left as far as the relationship between the - if I may say so - the mother organisation, which had its headquarters in Zagreb, and the other organisation, which had been created in Herzegovina. But I leave it as it is now, and it is up to the -- further study, probably, by anyone who is interested. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, there should be a clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment, please. As we are addressing a very important issue, there are several questions from the Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, excuse me. I would like to know the origin of this important political declaration that we're examining, 1D 02580. Which organ of the HDZ drafted this important political declaration? I see at the bottom of the page of the last page in English, it says "central board." And when I look at the statute of the HDZ, Article 28 in document 1D 02500 [as interpreted], among the bodies I do not come across the central board. So which is the authority which drafted and promulgated this political declaration, which is of great importance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in Article 28 of the statute, dated the 17th of December, 1993, it is clearly stated that the following bodies of the HDZ and BH, the Assembly, the Presidency, the main Board, the Central Board, the Executive Board, the Commission for Statutes, the Coat of Armour and the Auditing Board. If this mentioned declaration in document 580, the Central Board is mentioned, then this is a body of the HDZ which actually drafted and promulgated this political declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm told that in Article 28, number 4, it should -- it's been translated "central committee," but it should read "Central Board." In the original language, it's "Central Board," so that may be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I see. It's a problem of translation, then. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to come back to the previous question by the Judge [as interpreted] that the HDZ should become an integral part of the HDZ in Zagreb, and you answered something. Your answer opened up a path of reflection. You said that the HDZ was planet-wide, saying that there was HDZ organisations everywhere, Australia, et cetera. So if the HDZ is a planetary organisation like, for instance, the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, then there was the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia, of Hungary, the Communist Party of France, et cetera, et cetera, in its planetary dimension did the HDZ envisage that the seat of the HDZ should automatically be in Zagreb and the satellites could be in Bosnia-Herzegovina and elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot say that we were a satellite in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't think that we were a satellite of the HDZ of the Republic of Croatia. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, something is wrong with the sound. There's a mix-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll handle it. Apparently -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] We are hearing some very nasty comments from the translation booth, like, "Tudjman's vassals, Zdravko Batinic, satellite." So, please, this is what I heard, and all the others who can confirm this, from the translation booth, which indicates the personal political views of the interpreters, as Tudjman's vassals, Batinic was a satellite, and some other things along those lines. This is impermissible. If necessary, ask the others who are here present who could hear this when the microphone was turned on. So the interpreters are joining in with political views and assessments, and at this point in time I require an investigation, and I want the interpreters to be checked out. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was listening to the B/C/S booth, and I must say that what General Praljak has said is true. Obviously, the interpreters were having a private conversation in which they were making comments which certainly are inappropriate. The terms mentioned by Mr. Praljak were used and some others, and there was also some cynical comments regarding the witness that we have in the courtroom. And I believe the witness must have heard this, who is listening to the B/C/S, and all of us who are switched on to the sixth channel could hear this. So I'm just confirming the truthfulness of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And I was going to react before General Praljak did to confirm exactly what General Praljak indicated and my other colleague has indicated because of Ms. Tomanovic [sic]. At this point time in light of what is happening, I think we should take a break because I think that it's disrespectful and it's really abhorrent that at least now the Croats that are being tried in this Tribunal seem to be singled out by at least some of the interpreters. It may be -- it may be that something needs to be done, such as only those of a particular nation should be interpreting in this particular trial. Now, I think that would be devastating to this institution, but if, in fact, there are those within the booth that think that this is a laughing matter and where the gentleman himself can hear these comments, then I dare say this is a sad day for international criminal justice. And I just think that the best thing is take a break, perhaps look into the matter. We can take an early break. But I do think that this is unacceptable, and I believe the clients need to have a time-out for themselves to compose themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. We are grateful for this information. Maybe it's a bit of a consolation to the parties, in particular to the Defence, that the Judges have remained immune of all and any such comments because we do not listen to that language. So it has remained outside. This notwithstanding, I am quite shocked, I must say, of this, and I'm sure that the Chamber will deal with it. I would, as I have the floor, make an observation to the transcript. And on page 67 -- no -- yes, 67, line 21. Judge Antonetti has referred to Judge Prandler. I have heard this. And it just says "Judge" here. And as Mr. Mindua had spoken previously, I think it would be better to put this clear so that we know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are at your hands, but I do think that, again, it is very difficult to get witnesses here, precisely because the way some of them perceive this Tribunal to be acting. I'm not saying that those perceptions are accurate, but I do think that it's very difficult at times to get witnesses here, to put ten days of their life away, to be prepared, read documents, come here, answer questions under very difficult circumstances. And if the gentleman did indeed hear what apparently others heard in his own language, obviously at this point in time he must be wondering how or why he is here. You know, why is he bothering to come here to give evidence if those who are within this institution are mocking him, are mocking his heritage, are mocking his testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, what did you hear in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard somebody laughing, saying that Zdravko -- in these words, "Zdravko Batinic, a satellite," and some other words. I thought somebody in the courtroom was saying this. Fortunately, they were not. But what Mr. Karnavas said, and Mr. Praljak before him, is truly unacceptable. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one sentence. When he said, "to all intents and purposes," it's not so. I heard it, and I heard exactly what I said, laughter, with the words "Tudjman's vassals, Batinic is a satellite -- Tudjman satellite," laughter, "ironic," and "out of order."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to have a 20-minute break. Somebody wishes to intervene?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, I would. I would like to comment on Mr. Karnavas' expressions that witnesses that come here put ten days of their lives away. I think it's not a proper expression. They come here, they perform a duty, and I don't think one should intimate that to them entirely lost time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it's not lost. I don't mean to say that it is lost, but they're away from their families. They're away from their work. They're not getting compensated to be here. Trust me, Judge Trechsel, when I say that at least the witnesses that we bring over have to read a lot of documents, which is not very pleasant, and being questioned, even by myself on direct examination, can be intimidating, let alone being cross-examined. So that's what I meant. It is a public service. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. You can be assured of that, but then life is not only pleasure, and even toils are a part of life and can, all in all, have something rewarding, I think. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. But at least when they do come here, they should be treated properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But potential witnesses should not be told that "If you come to The Hague to testify, you're putting so-and-so many days of your life away." I think it's not encouraging, and we have to encourage them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we do have to warn them they're going to be here for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just a moment or two. I am also, as Judge Trechsel said, for better or worse, not in a position to directly comment on what was or was not being said in the translation booths or what was interpreted or not. I do note that the best record we have at the moment is what the witness himself, when asked by the Judge, "What did you hear," it wasn't very much. I mean, if that was the answer of the witness, he didn't indicate very much of any particular significance, other than the use of the word "satellite." I don't know -- again, I say I'm not in a position to comment, but I will observe for the record that when the witness was asked, it didn't seem particularly -- it did not seem particularly problematic. Be that as it may, whatever was said or not said, I think it's a gross overstatement and generalisation to then say that the Tribunal as a whole displays an anti-Croat bias. I think that's completely objectionable. It should not be heard in this courtroom. Mr. Praljak, when I'm finished, you can perhaps have the floor, if the Chamber wishes to give it to you. It is completely improper to say that. As far as the hardship on witnesses, Your Honour, I'm sure the Chamber will understand that every witness who comes here, including the many of the Bosniaks that came during the Prosecution case, come at considerable inconvenience and difficulty, as do the internationals, for that matter. So it would be improper to leave the impression -- two impressions on the record: Number 1, it's a gross overstatement and I think irresponsible to suggest the Tribunal is an anti-Croat tribunal, number 1; number 2, what Mr. Karnavas said about witnesses can be said about witnesses in general. Indeed, it may not be the most pleasant experience for everyone, but that applies across the board to all witnesses of every stripe, ethnic group, and political persuasion, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm convinced that this discussion is being recorded, and it would be a good idea for us to get a recording of this conversation. The Prosecutor is not telling the truth. There was even more said than what Mr. -- General Praljak said and Mr. Batinic and others in the courtroom here. A second point I wish to make here. Some witnesses who need to come here know years in advance that they are due to come. Be they victims or not, participants in that war, they have lost their -- their health has worsened, and my Defence has already noted that several witnesses will not be able to come because they're living with this trial; they're living with affected health. And when a witness is insulted in this way, it is unacceptable. This is an honourable act. Regardless of why those witnesses are coming here, they are witnesses of justice. They're not all professionals. They're not all intellectuals. They're ordinary people - I'm talking partly on behalf of my witnesses who will be coming here - who do not have great careers behind them, and one does not pay attention to the fact that for years they have been reflecting about these proceedings, and the rewards they get are shameful compared to some other rewards that are received by people here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak, just for a few seconds, and then we will have a break because this could go on forever. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I did not say that what I heard meant that the Tribunal or the Prosecution is anti-Croat. That is something I didn't say. The Prosecutor must have heard this alone. He often begins by saying, "I don't know, but ..." I think when someone says, "I don't know," one should keep quiet. If you didn't hear it or understand it, then, respected Mr. Prosecutor, keep quiet because things you don't know you should keep quiet about. Secondly, I clearly quoted not just the words but something that cannot be noticed from the recording, which makes a distinction between the written word and the spoken word. I will be referring to this later on when talking about transcripts. I conveyed truthfully and precisely what I heard. There were things I didn't quite understand, so I left them out. It is my opinion that the translation service is not suitable for interpretation. By their attitude towards Tudjman's vassals and Tudjman himself, this can lead to a whole series of misinterpretations. These may not be obvious but may emanate from their way of thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you have already said this and repeated it. You have intervened three times. Everyone has understood the issue. We're now going to have a 20-minute break, and we will resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So, first of all, a correction should be made. I'd like to provide you with some information with regard to what was said a while ago. The head of the interpretation department has replaced the interpreter and will be looking into the matter, will be conducting an investigation. That's all I can say at this point in time. My colleague has a correction he would like to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to point out something for the sake of the transcript. On page 67, line 3, with regard to the BH statute, I spoke about document 1D 02700 and not 2500, so that's a correction I would like to make to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry. I was on my feet just a moment ago. Thank you, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm happy to say that what Your Honour has said has very helpfully rather preempted and implemented what I on behalf of all Defences on this particular point, because we've discussed it over the break, was going to propose, that there should be some sort of inquiry or investigation into this matter. May we just add this, Your Honour, that discussions over the break -- and I'm not going to get at all into what's said. I certainly didn't hear a single word myself, nor would I have understood it. But without going into that at all, there is certainly reason to think that perhaps something slightly worse was said even than has been ventilated, but we don't know that for sure at the moment, Your Honour. But, Your Honour, we do suggest specifically, as part of this inquiry, that counsel and the accused, so far as they do have some input on this and do hear something, but the accused, through their counsel, that we, the Defences, should all be invited to submit to whoever is conducting this inquiry what we believe was said. That does seem to be a proper part of a proper inquiry into this particular matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The audio-recording is available to everyone, so the audio-recording should be consulted. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, I want to take you back to a remark that was made by Judge Prandler on page 66, line 15, in discussing the statute, which was 1D 02700, and upon your answer Judge Prandler indicated: "... The other organisation which had been created in Herzegovina." And from that I took to mean, since we're talking about the HDZ, that at least in the mind of -- unless this was a slip of tongue, that at least in the mind of some, the impression is that HDZ was a Herzegovinian creation. So let me ask you, was HDZ BH, was that an order created in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No. The HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina was established in Sarajevo, and it was for the entirety of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if I could take you on to the very last document, which is 1D 02701 [Realtime transcript read in error, "02001"]. This is the last document dealing with the HDZ. This is another statute. This is Mostar, 10 July 1994. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I don't want to spend too much time on it, but other than to make reference to the programatic declaration, as it said in English. That would be on page 21 in the English, 21, page 21 of this document. It's towards the end of your document, sir. It's the programme, essentially. I'm going to be looking at page 22. And at the very -- and this would be under Roman numeral II, where it says: "Basic goals and tasks of the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as set out in the programatic principles of the goals of the Croatian Democratic Union, accepted on the first general convention." And then it lists four items. Number 1, it says: "To ensure the right of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina to self-determination and statehood, independence and sovereignty in Bosnia-Herzegovina, a state union or constitutive nations." Can you please explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: This statute was adopted in 1994. The policies of the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina continued to be pursued, and this political declaration at the end of this statute refers to the desire we had, because usually declarations state one's desires and intentions, the desires and intentions of political parties. We wanted a Bosnia and Herzegovina as a union of peoples, and we wanted it to be suited to the Croatian people, as well, as we can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Unless there are any questions, I'll move on to the next topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, perhaps a correction to the transcript, because the document is indicated as 1D 02001. I have spent most of the time looking for it. In fact, I think it is 1D 02701.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct, 1D 02701. 1D 02701. And I was referring to page --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- 21 and going on to 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it lays out the principles. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, to follow up on what was just said, have a look at Article 2, which is very clear. It would appear the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina will have its headquarters in Sarajevo but when the state of war comes to an end. This text says that the headquarters of the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina will be located in Sarajevo, not in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is there an explanation? I guess that's the reason why it's being pointed out. I mean, we can all read that. Is there an explanation, well, now on July 10, 1994, it says "Sarajevo, when liberated," versus earlier? Do you have an explanation? If not, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: There's a very simple explanation for this. Having signed the Washington Agreement between the Croats and the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was no longer a state of war that prevailed. Peace was established between our two peoples, but war continued against the Serbian forces. At the time, Sarajevo was still occupied, and it wasn't possible to enter Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's go on to the next chapter, which deals with the HDZ Crisis Staff, Gornji Vakuf. That's how I've titled it, at least, for convenience sake. The first document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My attention is attracted to this Article 2, where I read of a confederation with the Republic of Croatia, and it is a bit puzzling. I wonder, Mr. Batinic, whether you could comment on that. To my knowledge, there is no such thing as a confederation between Bosnia and Herzegovina, on the one hand, and the Republic of Croatia, on the other hand, but it may be this is an error in translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, there is no confederation of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the Republic of Croatia, but this had been planned in the Washington Agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. I wasn't prepared to go into the Washington Agreement, but we can, Your Honours, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We can leave it at that, Mr. Karnavas. I'm sorry. It probably was known, but I know not all I should.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But It's -- I'm told that we could find it in Exhibit 1D 01530, Your Honour, if that may be of assistance. 1D 01530, which is in the exhibits already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next chapter, which is 1D 00485, 1D 00485, and we can see from this particular document -- first of all, do you recognise the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if we look at the end -- at the end of this document, we see President Stjepan Kljuic. I take it you knew the gentleman, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's look at the preamble. It says: "A session of the Security Council of the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina was held on 18 September 1991." First of all, can you tell us what, if anything, happened - noteworthy, that is - on that particular day in Bosnia-Herzegovina, 18 September 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 18th of December [as interpreted], 1991, the Serbian aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina commenced when the Serbians attacked the village of Ravno in Eastern Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Croatian village of Ravno.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, could you please explain to us, what is the Security Council of the Croatian Democratic Union?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The Security Council of the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina was a body that was supposed to take care of the safety of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina at a period of time when it seemed certain that the Serbian forces would launch an active aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, I don't want to go into this in any detail because I don't have the time, but if we could go to paragraph number 4, or item number 4, I should say, we can see that Stjepan Kljuic, it says: "... shall contact the leadership of the SDA without delay and ask them to state their policy, but the Crisis Staff shall develop an action plan with or without SDA and take specific steps in this direction." So now we have the words "Crisis Staff," and we could see that earlier. What exactly to your knowledge was being asked of Kljuic to do, and why?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: As the president of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Stjepan Kljuic at the time was told to establish contact with the political leadership of the SDA, the Party of Democratic Action, and having done so, to establish how the political leadership of the Muslims through the SDA Party saw how Bosnia-Herzegovina should be defended because they're prepared to participate. Why they're prepared to participate? Because the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina had commenced on that day when the Serbian forces attacked the Croatian village of Ravno.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, let's go on to the next document, unless there are any questions. I'll go on to the next document, which is 1D 00477. 1D 00477. And this is for the benefit -- to see what SDA was doing. This is dated 13 June 1991, and it's by - it says here: "The Council for National Defence of SDA has formed on Monday, 11 June, in Sarajevo." And it's signed by Hasan Cengic. Did you know Mr. Hasan Cengic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Not personally, but I know many things about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, who was he at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Hasan Cengic was a close associate of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic at the time. They both served prison sentences for being involved in the Young Muslims Movement. Later, he became the main logistics officer of the ABiH and dealt with obtaining weapons and equipment and financial means from Arab countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, obviously, this is several months before the previous document, when HDZ forms its Crisis Staff, and I pointed out number 4 where Kljujic is instructed to go talk to the leadership of the SDA. Let me ask you one simple question. At the time, were you aware that the SDA had already formed this Council for National Defence? Was it known?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: We found out about it a little later, a little after this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Can you -- do you recall, about when did you find out?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Midsummer 1991, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go on to the next chapter. This has -- just for convenience sake, it's titled "Kljuic and the Livno Question." If we go to document -- let's see. I'm sorry. I have to make sure that I don't make references to the documents that you handed over, but let me first ask you a question. Were you in Livno at all when the matter was discussed, that is, the so-called Livno question?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please tell us, why -- what is this all about? What was the question about, and why there was a controversy over it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Please, just tell me what the document number is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, the problem is -- I don't want to make reference to your notes because I can't use your notes in this courtroom because we can't use your diary. It's either all or nothing, I'm afraid, so you're going to have to go with your memory, although I will direct you at some point -- I will direct you at some point to P00117. That may be of some assistance. P00117. All right. Now, do you know why everyone convened on this particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you please tell us, and rather quickly, because I really -- I have limited time.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Just a couple of sentences with regard to what took place a week earlier. On the 2nd of February, 1992, in Siroki Brijeg, a meeting of the Central HDZ Committee [Transcript read in error, "SDA Central Committee"] of Bosnia and Herzegovina was held, an expanded meeting of this body, and there was discussion about the referendum on independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina that had been voted on. And the referendum did not satisfy most of the members of the Central Committee of the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina and this expanded version. The president of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina was criticised for not having sufficiently coordinated work with the HDZ representatives in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Slow down a bit, Mr. Batinic. This is very important because we already have one area where it says "SDA Central Committee," and we know we're talking about the HDZ. So -- all right. There was an issue with the coordination. What was the problem? Get to the issue.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The problem was a problem that concerned the referendum by the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a referendum that people had voted in. Most of the members of the Central Committee of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not agree with it. Mr. Kljujic was criticised for not having sufficiently thought through the issue, in political terms. He hadn't made enough effort and hadn't coordinated the representatives of the HDZ in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He hadn't coordinated his activities. Such an issue shouldn't have been put forth at the Assembly. The representatives of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina shouldn't have supported such an issue in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Why? Because the referendum at the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, according to most of the members of the Central Committee, was prejudicial to the internal structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, according to the members of the Central Committee of the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the referendum concerned an issue inside Bosnia and Herzegovina. For all of these reasons, Mr. Kljujic felt that he no longer had the support of most of the members of the Central Committee; and as a result, he resigned. When the committee continued to sit -- well, the committee met seven days later in Livno, and at that meeting the question for the referendum was formulated, and it was supposed to be put before the SDA, and an attempt was to be made in the Assembly to change the issue, the result. Unfortunately, the representatives of the SDA were not in favour of changing the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we know, from having heard from previous witnesses, that at some point Kljujic was no longer the president of the HDZ. Could you please tell us, how did that come about?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kljujic resigned at the session of the Central Committee of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Siroki Brijeg on the 2nd of February, 1992. He had understood that he no longer had the support of that body when it came to leading the HDZ in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Instead of "to change the issue," it should state "to change the question."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, just getting -- let's look at this one document, P00117. This is 9 February 1992. And if we look on page 2 in the English version, we can see the proposed -- we see, under item 3: "Referendum on sovereign and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina," and we see the following: "Are you in favour of a sovereign and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, a joint state of the constitutive and sovereign Croatian, Muslim and Serbian peoples in their ethnic areas," and in brackets it says "(cantons)?" Was that the question as you recall it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I was at this session of the Central Board of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Livno, and in my diaries I made a note of the question: "Are you in favour of a sovereign and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, a joint state of the constituent and sovereign Croatian, Muslim and Serbian peoples?" I'm not claiming that this text before us wasn't drafted as such, but what I heard is what I put down in my personal diary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: The witness is referring to his diaries, and as Counsel Karnavas said as we started after the recess, it's got to be either/or or nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, let me lay a foundation. Are you testifying on the basis of your memory?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I'm testifying about this on the basis of my memory and also on the basis of what is contained in my personal notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's kind of difficult to unring the bell. I don't know whether he remembered that in advance and now he's looked at his notes, but in any event, he was entitled to refresh his memory even before coming here. We're not using his notes, which were taken contemporaneous at the time, and I can ask him that question, but he's testifying from his memory. Let me go on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With respect to cantons, since we do have the word "cantons" in this particular question, so whether it was inclusive or whether -- in the original question or whether it was part of an explanation, what was meant by "cantons"?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No one was very clear about that or said anything about this. At the session, when the matter was discussed, cantons were discussed in general terms or, rather, national areas, and no one mentioned any figures when it came to cantons or any areas. In this question, in this referendum for Bosnia and Herzegovina, all I wanted to do was to see what the internal structure should be if it was also to suit the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you talked about there was a previous meeting on 2nd of February, 1992. Were any foreign guests at that meeting that you recall, that you recall?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: At the session of the Central Board of the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 2nd of February in Siroki Brijeg, our most distinguished guest was the president of the Executive Committee of the HDZ for the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Stjepan Mesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recall -- I want you to testify from your memory. Do you recall what, if anything, he said at the meeting? In other words, did he address the attendants, and if so, in what capacity, and what, if anything, he might have said that sticks out in your mind today.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stjepan Mesic took the floor on a number of occasions. The essence of what he had to say as the president of the Executive Board for the HDZ for the Republic of Croatia was -- well, that he wanted to express the official position of the HDZ in Croatia, and according to the official position, the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina should support the referendum with regard to an independent and sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, since he was present and since the question or the essence of the question was being discussed, did he take a position one way or the other with respect to the question, or was he simply urging people to just go and vote, irrespective of the nature of the question?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: He expressed the official position of the HDZ of the Republic of Croatia, given that he was acting in the capacity of president of the Executive Board of the HDZ in the Republic of Croatia, and these were acts that were carried out in the policies of the HDZ in Croatia. So there was no incitement here, as you put it. This was just the official position of the HDZ in the Republic of Croatia. With regard to the referendum, since you have touched on this issue, I have to emphasise the fact that all the members of the Central Committee board who were present or the Central Board who were present were in favour of a referendum of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, but they wanted the question to be rephrased. The question put at the referendum, according to them, should have been rephrased.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at the last document in this bundle, which is 1D 00410, 1D 00410. This is from a text by Miroslav Tudjman. It's a compilation of various documents, and if I could draw your attention. For us in the English version, it would be at the very -- at the right-hand top of the page, it says "141, Cutileiro plan proposed HDZ BiH..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This would be the fourth page, Your Honours, the fourth page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you have that document in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, of course, we can see that the source of this document -- in the footnote, it says "HINA." Do you know what this source is?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The Croatian Information News Agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And it appears that Miro Lasic, the head of the HDZ delegation, is made reference to, as well as Mate Boban. And if we look at this text, it says that the -- under paragraph 2, the: "Basic HDZ demand in maintaining BiH within its historical borders, which are today's borders, as well as an independent and sovereign state of three constitutive and sovereign nations and citizens who live in that territory. According to the HDZ proposal, Bosnia and Herzegovina would be, as multinational unity, the state with divided sovereignty; one would belong to the cantonal authorities, and the other to the central confederative authority. Every authority would be sovereign in its own domain." I want to skip the rest of the part. There are some interested passages in the next paragraph, but due out of time, I won't cover that. But if we go to the third-from-the-last paragraph, the paragraph third from the bottom, it talks about a model for the government status, which HDZ deligacy proposed in Lisbon, is well known and implemented in a sovereign world in different variants: United States of America, Switzerland, Belgium, and others. Can you please tell us, having looked at this document, whether what is reflected in here as far as the future governmental status of BiH is consistent with or inconsistent with HDZ's policy as you understood it to be when the negotiations were taking place concerning the Livno question?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: This is absolutely in line with the programme declaration of the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina and in line with the proposal for the referendum proposed by members of the Central Board of the HDZ for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, finally, before we leave this Livno question, the referendum question: At that meeting on the 2nd or, later on, on the 9th of February, were there any maps, any documents, draft constitutions, charters, statutes, anything that would assist the participants in figuring out what it was that the Croats were asking?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next chapter --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, if we could just take a little detour. Your Honours, I have 1D 01530, which is the Law on the Ratification of the Preliminary Agreement of the Establishment of the Confederation between the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia, and I have it here in hard copy for the Judges to look at. Unless there are any questions regarding the confederation issue that was discussed earlier, I'll go on to the next chapter, "Arming the Muslims." That's what the title is. It doesn't necessarily mean anything special, but 1D 02445. 1D 02445. This is 8 April 1992, we can see, and this is from Srebrenik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know where Srebrenik is?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: The Municipality of Srebrenik is in the northeast of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And can you please tell us what the makeup of this municipality is, based on the nationality quota?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: According to the population census of 1991 for Bosnia and Herzegovina, more than 40.000 inhabitants were in Srebrenik, more than 30.000 of which stated that they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And over here -- now, during that period of time, do you have any firsthand knowledge whether the Republic of Croatia was providing military assistance to municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, particularly municipalities that were predominantly made up of the Muslim nation?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I do not have firsthand knowledge of this, but it was common knowledge that the Republic of Croatia was assisting the Muslims of Bosnia and Herzegovina with weapons and equipment in order to defend themselves from the Serb aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document, which is 1D 02443. This deals with Konjic. And if we look at the end of the document, we will all recognise the gentleman's name, Dr. Rusmir Hadzihuseinovic. I think I got it right. This is dated 12 April 1992, and correct me if I'm wrong. I don't want to lead you too much, but is Konjic next to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And do you happen to know what the -- based on the census, more or less what the makeup of Konjic municipality was?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Konjic municipality had a majority Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And did you know this gentleman that is mentioned as the president of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We'll go on to the next series of documents, and this deals more in line with Gornji Vakuf, so that's why I titled it just that. And as I understand, it's a very -- we'll start off with 1D 03104. This is dated 7 April 1992. We see it's a conclusion, and we see at the bottom that it's by the president of the Crisis Staff, Muhamed Palalic. Did you know Mr. Palalic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And up until what time, period of time, was Mr. Palalic the president of the crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Mr. Palalic was president of the Crisis Staff and president of the Presidency of Gornji Vakuf municipality until the 16th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And prior to becoming the president of the Crisis Staff, what position did Mr. Palalic hold?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Mr. Palalic was president of the Assembly of Gornji Vakuf Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall whether you were present during this particular meeting, 7 April 1992, when these conclusions were drawn?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: I remember perfectly well. I was present at this meeting of the Crisis Staff because the meeting was being held in the evening of the 7th of April, 1992, and during that same day the Crisis Staff for Gornji Vakuf municipality was formed pursuant to a decision of the Assembly, and Mr. Palalic was appointed president and Zdravko Batinic deputy president, in other words, myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just very quickly, on the first item, it talks about: "Group of operatives consisting of three representatives of the Crisis Staff of the Croatian Democratic Union, Gornji Vakuf Municipality, HDZ Committee, and three representatives of the Crisis Staff of the BiH Patriotic League of the Gornji Vakuf municipality ..." Do you see that part? "... give a proposal for the compositions of names for the operative staff..."

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: " ... the operative staff of Territorial Defence." Could you please explain to us, what was the operative staff of Territorial Defence of the Gornji Vakuf was about? What was its functions, or what was its functions supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Three representatives of the Crisis Staff of the HDZ for Gornji Vakuf municipality and three representatives of the Patriotic League were meant to set up an operative staff for Gornji Vakuf municipality, which would work on the mobilisation and defence of Gornji Vakuf municipality against Serb aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Unless there are any questions from the Bench --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Unless there are any questions from the Bench, I will go on to the next document, which is 1D 03105. This is dated now 15 May 1992, and this is a conclusion. And we see at the -- this conclusion, it says; it's from the Crisis Staff: "A joint command or a military coordinating body between the HVO Command and the Municipal/Territorial Defence." Did that ever occur; was this conclusion ever materialised; and if so, to what extent ?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. It came about in the form of a military coordinating body. The Command of the HVO -- of the armed forces of the HVO for Gornji Vakuf municipality and the Command of the armed forces of the TO coordinated their activities along the defence lines for the Municipality of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document, 1D -- well, let me ask you this before we go to the next document because this may be of importance: How long did that cooperation last? Up to what point?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: Until the 11th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Of course, you did indicate that prior to January 11th, 1993, there were the two incidents, the one in June and then the one in October, and so I guess it begs the question: If the cooperation was ongoing, why did those two incidents occur?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: It is hard to explain this. I said a few sentences linked to the 20th of June, 1992, and the 24th of October, 1992, but after these few days, these forces resumed coordination along the defence lines on the mountain of Radus against the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At that point in time, who was the head of the HVO and who was the head of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC
utterances.text: In the -- from the 15th of May, the commander of the HVO for Gornji Vakuf municipality was Mr. Pero Medandzic [phoen], and the commander of the armed forces of the TO was Mr. Fikret Musa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.
